hints: Notice the three family names in the options: hadron, baryon and meson - recall which one is the large group containing the other two.
Connect quark content to the subgroups: a proton is $uud$, so ask whether three quarks means a baryon or a quark-antiquark meson.
Check whether baryon and meson can overlap - if a particle is made of three quarks, can it also count as a meson?
walkthrough: Identify the particle: a proton has quark composition $uud$, so it is made of three quarks and feels the strong force.
State the governing rule: hadrons are particles made of quarks that interact via the strong force.
Split hadrons into two exclusive subgroups: baryons are made of three quarks ($qqq$) and mesons are made of one quark and one antiquark ($q\bar{q}$).
Apply the rule to the proton: $uud$ matches the $qqq$ baryon pattern and does not match the $q\bar{q}$ meson pattern.
Conclude that the proton is a hadron of the baryon type only, so it is a baryon but not a meson. This is option A.

options.A: A proton is made of three quarks ($uud$) so it is a baryon, and baryons and mesons are mutually exclusive classes.
options.B: A proton cannot be a meson because a meson is a quark-antiquark pair, and every meson is also a hadron.
options.C: A proton is a hadron, but hadrons split into baryons or mesons and a proton with three quarks is not a meson.
options.D: A particle cannot be both classes at once - a proton with quark content $uud$ is a baryon, not a quark-antiquark meson.
